what: 2 footnotes; reviewers' fixes (2026-11-03 review: facts, quiz items, no lesson numbers)
notes: Physics fix: 'the Sun peaks in the green' depends on how the spectrum is plotted (per unit wavelength it peaks near 500 nm; per unit frequency in the near infrared). Remove it as a bare fact from the hook, summary, key ideas and quiz explanations. The no-green-stars argument rests on the glow's breadth: a broad hump always gives the eye's three kinds of colour receptor plenty to see, so the mix runs from reddish through white to bluish and is never green alone.

Physics fix: the quiz item 'An iron bar and a lump of glass are heated to the same high temperature. Their glow: has about the same colour' is wrong for clear glass, which absorbs poorly and so glows feebly. Change the materials to an iron bar and a brick (both good absorbers), keeping the answer.
Add one line: in everyday symbols red means hot and blue cold (taps, weather maps), but for glowing things blue is hotter.
Scope 'can never be green' to glowing hot bodies (lasers, LEDs and emeralds can be green for other reasons).
Make 'depends on its temperature and nothing else' agree with the key idea that it depends 'hardly at all on what it's made of' (true for good absorbers like iron and brick).

what: 2 footnotes; reviewers' fixes (2026-11-03 review: facts, quiz items, no lesson numbers)
notes: Kelvin's 1862 estimate: the Sun had probably not lit the Earth for 100 million years, and almost certainly not for 500 million; his '20 to 30 million' came later. Fix the text, key ideas, quiz and the timeline label ('1862 Kelvin: the Sun is at most a few tens of millions of years old'), consistent with Geology lesson 8.
Attribution: Gamow's 1928 tunnelling explained alpha particles escaping nuclei; Robert Atkinson and Fritz Houtermans applied tunnelling to fusion in stars in 1929.

Fix 'a fuel that turns thousandths of its mass into light' (text and key ideas): fusion turns 0.7 per cent of the hydrogen burned into energy; over its whole life the Sun turns well under a thousandth of its total mass into light. The 'million times better than coal' comparison can stay.
Make clear that 'the Sun could shine for about ten billion years' is the modern figure, not Eddington's 1920 estimate.
Shorten the Darwin/Weald paragraph to a sentence plus the existing link to Geology lesson 8, which tells that story.
